description: If your child was hurt at a private school in Georgia, the immunity wall that protects public schools is gone. What is left is ordinary negligence law.
shortAnswer: If your child was hurt at a private school, almost none of Georgia’s school immunity applies to you. The wall is gone. What is left is the ordinary question every other injury case asks: did the people in charge use reasonable care?

sections.heading: What falls away at a private school
sections.shortAnswer: A private academy is not the State. There is no fight over whether supervising children was “discretionary” or “ministerial,” no need to prove actual malice, and no ante litem notice to a city or county.

sections.heading: What a private school will argue instead
sections.shortAnswer: Charitable immunity does not protect a charity from a beneficiary who pays for the service, and tuition is payment. A release cannot excuse gross negligence or willful and wanton conduct.

sections.heading: Bullying: aim at the school, not only the other child’s parents
sections.shortAnswer: O.C.G.A. § 51-2-3 makes a parent liable for a child’s willful or malicious acts, but only up to $10,000 plus court costs. At a private school, the school is usually the defendant who matters.

sections.heading: Heat illness and cardiac events: the sequel to Return to Play
sections.shortAnswer: At a private school, the question is whether the coach used reasonable care, and these written rules are the best evidence of what a reasonable coach knew to do.

sections.heading: School bus stops: the loading zone is where the duty is clearest
sections.shortAnswer: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-164 says a driver who stops to let children off may not move the bus until all children who need to cross the roadway have done so safely.

sections.heading: What I tell private school parents to do
sections.shortAnswer: Get the enrollment contract, the athletic packet, and the handbook. Gather every email, text, and note you sent the school before the injury. Protect both claims inside the ordinary two years.

faq.q: Can a private school in Georgia claim sovereign or official immunity when a child is hurt?
faq.a: No. A private academy is not the State. A teacher at a church school is not a public officer. The Supreme Court of Georgia held in Hartley v. Agnes Scott College, 295 Ga. 458 (2014), that even the police officers of a private college were not state officers entitled to immunity.

faq.q: Does a release in a Georgia private school enrollment contract stop an injury claim?
faq.a: A release cannot excuse gross negligence or willful and wanton conduct. Whether a parent’s signature can waive the child’s own claim for ordinary negligence is not settled by a Georgia appellate court. An arbitration clause is a fight, not a forfeit.

faq.q: Is a private school liable when a bully seriously injures my child in Georgia?
faq.a: The school took charge of your child. It owes reasonable care commensurate with the foreseeable risk. Georgia courts measure foreseeability by what the school knew about this child’s propensity for this kind of harm. In a bullying case, that paper trail is the case.

faq.q: Do Georgia’s sudden cardiac arrest rules for student athletes apply to private schools?
faq.a: Yes. The Jeremy Nelson and Nick Blakely Sudden Cardiac Arrest Prevention Act covers public and private schools with any of grades 6 through 12. A student who faints must be removed from play. Georgia’s 2024 law requiring defibrillators and cardiac emergency plans in schools covers public schools only.
